extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors in a research ethics seminar (COMP 601/CAAM 601)
extracted.subtask_description: A short case-summary used in a research ethics seminar describing the Ford Pinto's known safety defect, internal testing results, company policy, and the cost–benefit analysis that led Ford not to adopt an inexpensive fix. The page is intended to prompt ethical analysis of corporate decision-making about product safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of a dangerous design flaw via crash testing
rubrics_metrics.description: During crash tests which preceded the introduction of the Pinto to the public, it became apparent that the vehicle had a dangerous design flaw: the gas tank was so designed and located that when it was involved in a rear end collision at an impact speed of 20mph or higher, the tank was apt to rupture, causing a fire or explosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page specifies the conditions in which the flaw manifested (rear-end collisions ≥20 mph) and the mechanical causes (tank five inches forward of rear sheet metal, three inches back of axle housing; axle housing deformation and protruding bolts puncturing the tank). Use of concrete test-results and mechanistic explanation is shown as the basis for evaluating the safety problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of specific structural/design contributors to failure
rubrics_metrics.description: The tank was only five inches forward of the rear sheet metal of the body and only three inches back of the rear axle housing; in most of the rear-end crash tests the axle housing deformed the tank and sharp, protruding bolts punctured the tank. In only 20 mph moving barrier crashes, the rear end crush distance was large--more than eight inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed measurements and descriptions of deformation are presented as relevant evidence for judging the severity and mechanical cause of the defect; evaluators should note exact spatial relationships, deformation modes, and measured crush distances when assessing design safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of low-cost corrective measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested changes to repair the defects were not expensive, something in the range of $11 per car.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights that a relatively inexpensive engineering change was available (~$11/vehicle). When evaluating corporate responses, the availability and per-unit cost of feasible fixes is an important criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company policy restricting adoption of safety features until legally required
rubrics_metrics.description: A confidential company policy memo issued in late 1971, directed that no additional safety features be adopted for the 1973 and later cars until required by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational policy that prohibits voluntary safety upgrades is presented as a factual constraint on action; evaluators should consider how internal policies interact with ethical obligations and regulatory timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cost–benefit analysis to decide against implementing fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: A cost-benefit analysis prepared by Ford concluded that it was not cost-effecient to add an $11 per car cost in order to correct the flaws. Benefits derived from spending this amount of money were estimated to be $49.5 million... When the unit cost was spread out over the number of cars and light trucks which would be affected by the design change, at a cost of $11 per vehicle, the cost was calculated to be $137 million, much greater then the $49.5 million benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page shows a concrete application of monetary cost–benefit reasoning as the decisive factor. Evaluations should examine how costs and aggregated benefits were computed and whether the approach properly accounts for non-monetary or moral considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary valuation of human life and injury in benefit calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: This estimate assumed that each death which could be avoided would be worth $200,000, that each major burn injury that could be avoided would be worth $67,000 and that an average repair cost of $700 per car involved in a rear end accident would be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents specific dollar values assigned to deaths and injuries used in Ford's benefit estimate. Scrutiny should be applied to the choice of valuation figures and the ethical implications of assigning monetary value to human life and injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on assumed incident frequencies in projecting benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: It further assumed that there would be 2,100 burned vehicles, 180 serious burn injuries, and 180 burn deaths in making this calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The benefit side depended on assumed counts of incidents and casualties. Evaluations should assess the source, reasonableness, and uncertainty of these incidence estimates and how sensitive outcomes are to those assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit ethical question of failing to adopt known safety improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Ford's conclusion and policy — having known test results, an inexpensive fix, and a decision not to implement it — frames an ethical issue about corporate responsibility to adopt safety improvements versus minimizing costs absent legal compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although presented as narrative fact, this entry signals the normative criterion: whether it is ethically acceptable to refrain from safety changes that are inexpensive and would reduce deaths/injuries. Use the documented facts (tests, cost, memo, analysis) to reason about duties, culpability, and policy reform.
